title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
This page is part of Euler's practical primality test using idoneal numbers (numeri idonei). If n is idoneal and gcd(x,y)=1, a number N = n·x² + y² is prime exactly when it has only one such representation, provided some further conditions hold. A second representation gives a factor.

(1) The page opens with the end of the previous example, 64013 in the form 40aa+13bb. The numbers subtracted have differences that fall by 1040 = 2·40·13 at each step: 1640, 600, −440, −1480, −2520. No remainder is a square, so 64013 is declared prime.

(2) §58–59 give a larger example using the idoneal number 840. Take N = 999601 = 840·34² + 169². To look for other representations, Euler computes 999601 − 840x² for x = 0, 1, 2, …. He does no multiplications: he subtracts the odd multiples (2x+1)·840 in turn. These differences grow by 1680 at each step. The two columns run from x = 0 to x = 34. Beyond that, 840·35² > N, so the search is complete.

(3) Two squares appear among the remainders.
- At x = 7 the remainder is 958441 = 979².
- At x = 34 the remainder is 28561 = 169², the known representation.
So 999601 = 840·7² + 979² = 840·34² + 169², and N is composite.

(4) Euler's fraction rule (as used on the next page) gives the factor.
- p/q = (34+7)/(979+169) = 41/1148 = 1/28, so 840 + 784 = 1624 = 8·7·29.
- p/q = (34−7)/(979−169) = 27/810 = 1/30, so 840 + 900 = 1740 = 4·3·5·29.
Both contain 29, and indeed 999601 = 29·34469, where 34469 is prime. The factorisation is presumably given on the following page of the original.
errors: None found. I recomputed every subtraction in both columns (999601 → 998761 → … → 958441 = 979² → … → 756841 → … → 84841 → 28561 = 169²) and all are correct.

ideas.what: Primality test: a number is prime if it has a unique representation n x² + y² with n idoneal (convenient)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E708, E715, E719, E725 and letters to Lagrange and Béguelin, c. 1778)
ideas.where_published: Nova Acta Petrop. papers on numeri idonei; E719 (1805)

ideas.what: Searching all representations by subtracting successive odd multiples of n, i.e. a first-difference table of n x²
ideas.modern_name: Method of differences / sieve-like search for representations by a binary quadratic form

ideas.what: Extracting a factor from two representations via the fraction (a±x)/(b±y)
ideas.modern_name: Factoring from two representations by a quadratic form (Euler's factoring method)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (for sums of two squares, and for general idoneal forms)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine worked example of Euler's well-documented idoneal-number primality test. The numbers are correct and nothing on the page is new to the literature.
transcription_corrections: The section after the table is printed '§. 60' (in the scan it may read like '66'); the sequence §58, §59 implies §60.
The '[?]' after '840xx + yy' in §58 is unnecessary: the image reads 'in forma idonea 840xx + yy contineatur'.
In §58 the image reads 'sine pluris ambagibus' with long-s ('fine'); the meaning is 'without much circumlocution'.
The top-of-page differences are 1640, 600, −440, −1480, −2520 (step −1040); the transcription's dashes between −440 and −1480 should read as minus signs separated by commas.
